title: DC Comics Now Sits Within Skydance Products & Publishing Division Under Josh Silverman, Alongside Warner Bros. and Paramount Consumer Products Groups
description: The new Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, has consolidated its publishing and consumer-products teams into o
body:
The new Skydance, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, has consolidated its publishing and consumer-products teams into one group — Skydance Products & Publishing — led by Josh Silverman.

	Silverman, who joined Paramount Skydance in 2025 as president of global products and experiences, now serves as president of global products and publishing for Skydance. Robert Oberschelp, president of global consumer products at Warner Bros. Discovery, for now is remaining with the new Skydance, reporting to Silverman. 
	

	According to Skydance, with the combination of Paramount and Warner Bros., the company is now the world’s second-largest media and entertainment licensor (after Disney) with an estimated $22.5 billion in global retail sales.


	DC Comics will come under Silverman’s leadership alongside Paramount Global Publishing, Paramount and WBD licensed publishing, WBD consumer products and Paramount consumer products, as well as brand partnerships, retail and e-commerce, and other commercial initiatives across the company’s portfolio of brands. 



	

					Josh Silverman
	



	Skydance Products & Publishing, working with the company’s TV and film divisions, is responsible for managing licensing for brands and franchises including Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings, DC, Star Trek, SpongeBob SquarePants, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Hanna-Barbera and Looney Tunes, among others.

	Prior to joining Paramount last year, Silverman was chief franchise officer of Mattel, where he expanded the company’s global consumer products and publishing businesses and oversaw more than 165 consumer product partnerships tied to the “Barbie” movie. He also has held senior leadership roles at Disney, including as EVP of global third-party commercialization leading consumer product licensing, and Marvel Entertainment.
	

	Read Silverman’s note to the division’s staffers, sent on Tuesday (Oct. 2) when the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger closed:

	Team,

	Today marks a historic milestone, the first day of our new company, Skydance, and our organization, Skydance Products & Publishing. I want to welcome you and share some information about the road ahead.

	I am honored to lead this division, bringing together Consumer Products, Publishing, and DC, and look forward to getting to know you.

	The combination of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery creates a next generation tech-forward global media and entertainment company with endless opportunity. It also represents significant change. I recognize that many of you have questions about what comes next. Please know your day-to-day work and processes won’t change immediately. We are beginning the integration process which will be approached thoughtfully. I am committed to keeping you informed and sharing updates as soon as possible.

	What is already clear is the tremendous talent across our organization and our shared mission to deepen and extend our fans’ emotional connection to our iconic brands and franchises through high-quality products and stories. Through our globally connected ecosystem, partnerships and world-class storytelling and world-building, your work brings our brands to life and plays an important role in the company’s success.

	I want to recognize Robert Oberschelp and the Warner Bros. Discovery Consumer Products team and the strong foundation they have built.

	I also want to welcome Anne DePies, Jim Lee and all of DC and celebrate the incredible way they have continued to engage audiences for generations.

	I look forward to working with Robert, Anne and Jim and their respective teams as we unite the strengths of both studios, create new opportunities for our partners, and unlock new ways to connect with fans who remain at the heart of everything we do.

	As you heard in this morning’s global Town Hall, David and Ynon are very clear on the vision, mission, and strategic priorities for Skydance. If you were unable to join, I encourage you to watch the replay available on the Skydance Integration Hub, which will serve as a go-to source for updates, FAQs, and other information as we progress through this transition.
	

	I’m looking forward to the journey and excited about what we will achieve together in this next chapter.

	Best,

	Josh

title: Bela Bajaria on Netflix’s Epic TV Trek into Local Language Production: ‘There’s No Roadmap for This’
description: Bela Bajaria was a few months into her job as the leader of Netflix’s international content expansion campaign in 2019 when she fully realized the s
body:
Bela Bajaria was a few months into her job as the leader of Netflix’s international content expansion campaign in 2019 when she fully realized the significance of the opportunity ahead.

	The production of local original content was not destined to be a side business for Netflix — it is the business, and increasingly so as the world’s largest subscription streaming platform relies on growth outside the U.S. to drive future profits. Netflix’s oft-stated goal is to be the platform that has something for every subscriber and every viewing mood — morning, noon and night. By that definition, Netflix has to invest enormous resources in programs, films and events that matter to subscribers. And that can’t be done all in English for a global subscription platform that reaches 190-plus countries (and transacts business in 45 currencies).
	

	“There’s no road map for this — local programming is unprecedented at this scale,” Bajaria, now Netflix’s chief content officer, tells Variety.


	For the extraordinary contributions made by Netflix to the global content landscape, Bajaria will receive the Vanguard Award from Variety and Mipcom during the international content marketplace and summit that runs Oct. 12-15 in Cannes. The kudo will be presented at the Palais des Festivals on Oct. 12 and will include an onstage conversation with Cynthia Littleton, Variety’s co-editor in chief.

	“We understand that great storytelling can come from anywhere, and now the discovery and technology give you access to all of these stories from around the world,” Bajaria says. “Every Netflix production is a very deeply local production — that means from local creative executives in that creative community who live there, who speak the language, who grew up in that business.”
	

	Today, Netflix has a $20 billion content budget and offices in 27 countries. The streamer produces TV and original movies in 50 different languages for more than 50 countries. It also commissions thousands of hours of local-language content each year. Shonda Rhimes, the powerhouse show runner who signed on with Netflix in 2017, calls Bajaria “decisive” and “frank” in ways that mesh well with her own style.

	“There’s not ever an issue when you’re talking to her and she’s afraid to act. Especially in this era we’re in with television, and everybody’s feeling so uncertain, it’s very rare to spend time with a decisive person like that,” Rhimes tells Variety. “I love being able to talk to somebody who can give me a definitive yes or no. Bela’s that person.”

	Bajaria came to Netflix in 2016 to spearhead the streamer’s push into unscripted content. That was a big professional shift for someone who’d spent most of her career in scripted TV, over more than 15 years at CBS and later as the head of NBC’s Universal Television.

	Bajaria grew up in London and in Zambia before her family relocated to Torrance when she was 9. In 2019, when she was promoted to lead Netflix’s international originals strategy, Bajaria seized the unique chance to assemble a worldwide network of content hubs.

	Bajaria got out her passport and hit the road (and the skies) to meet with producers and executives in far-flung corners. It was exhilarating, she recalls. Her travel schedule has not let up since.

	“I’ve been at Netflix for almost 10 years. Netflix has grown a lot over the last decade, but the ambition and the goal have always been the same: We want to be the most creative entertainment company in the world,” says Bajaria. “When we started opening the country offices and hiring local teams, we always wanted to have shows and films that people loved, no matter which country they lived in, the language they speak or whatever mood they were in.”

	In 2019, the rationale was that “to become a global company and to do local storytelling, it’s going to take the investment and local hiring. It wasn’t really one region at a time. We had a few pockets of people in different regional offices, but it was like OK, even if we have people in Singapore for Asia, we really need a Tokyo office, a Seoul office, a Bangkok office. In India, we had a couple of people in Mumbai, but it really was more U.S. people, so we went in and started to build it up,” Bajaria recalls.
	

	Typically, Bajaria focused on hiring a plugged-in creative executive with great contacts. The arrival of Netflix in many regions, including South Korea and areas of Africa, has been a watershed moment that helped turbocharge local production infrastructure, jobs and expenditures. At present, the company has done business with more than 2,000 local production outfits during the last 10 years.

	Bajaria was promoted to chief content officer in January 2023, taking oversight of Netflix original films as well as TV series, live events and a burgeoning lineup of sports rights. She may oversee the biggest programming slate in the history of moving pictures, but she’s never too busy to weigh in when asked and to be forthcoming when it matters most, in Rhimes’ experience.

	RELATED STORY: How Netflix’s Chief Content Officer was Born to Disrupt the Status Quo

	“She’s very frank with me,” Rhimes says. “I don’t do well with platitudes, and I don’t do well with people talking in metaphors or trying to say something in a passive way. Bela’s like ‘That didn’t work for me,’ and I really appreciate that in a world in which I think most people don’t want to tell you exactly what they think.”

	Rhimes moved her company’s home base to Netflix from Disney in 2017, about 18 months after Netflix threw open its doors to international business in January 2016.

	Today, Netflix, as of its latest disclosures, counts about 95 million subscribers in the U.S. and Canada, or about 29% of its 325 million total subscribers at the end of 2025. Europe, the Middle East and Africa combined account for about 109 million subscribers, followed by Asia-Pacific (65 million) and Latin America (59 million).

	Rhimes says there’s a special kind of cultural wallop that comes from launching a show on the scale of “Bridgerton” or 2022’s “Inventing Anna” on a platform that offers simultaneous global reach. Rhimes’ previous hit dramas, such as ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy” and “Scandal,” traveled the world but never with the impact of being available everywhere all at once, a la “Bridgerton.”

	Year one of the costume drama set in Regency-era England — which dropped on Christmas Day 2020 — rocketed star Regé-Jean Page to stardom. The experience opened up Rhimes’ vision for storylines and backdrops for Shondaland’s creations.
	

	“That was such a tremendous feeling to know that it was conversation everywhere — literally globally,” Rhimes says of the “Bridgerton” bow. “There’s something about it that allows me to think less in terms of American stories and more in terms of placing things in a more international way.”

	Bajaria is quick to reel off statistics that give a sense of Netflix’s scope.

	Among other notable numbers:


Netflix has generated 425,000 production jobs around the world in 10 years. 
In Mexico, Netflix does biz with more than 50 local production companies. They’ve committed to spending $1 billion on content targeted for Mexico from 2025-2028.
Netflix has committed $2.5 billion to spend on Korean content from 2023-2027.



	How in the world does Bajaria keep up with it all? As a veteran creative executive, she also knows how to pick the right time to get involved on a detail level with programs.

	“When I click play, I’m watching it as fresh eyes,” she says. “There’s no great plan for why I watch this or I don’t watch that. [Netflix executives] send things to me. As I’m traveling, I’m watching something constantly. The interesting thing is — either you get transported and engaged in the story, or you don’t. It’s never, ‘Well, it must be because of a language barrier or it’s culturally specific.’ No, the show or the movie just didn’t work. Storytelling is universal. Either you go for the ride or you don’t.”

	Bajaria emphasizes that the focus is on developing regional and language-specific hits and to seed franchises that keep subscribers engaged. When a local-language program or movie blows up, a la Korea’s “Squid Game” or France’s “Lupin” or, early on, Spain’s “La Casa de Papel,” it’s a gamechanger for viewership and subscribers.

	But the shows first and foremost have to connect with local audiences.

	“There’s always this constant at the end of the day. Whether you’re in São Paulo or London or Bangkok, there’s a filmmaker or creator who has a vision and something to say and you back that vision. Ultimately that is the core part of the job we do — supporting the vision or storytelling,” Bajaria says.

	“There’s great fandom for anime that we make from Japan, and people love Korean content. And there’s definitely times when people discover something like ‘Chestnut Man’ from the Nordics or ‘Blood of Sacrifice’ from Sweden. Then they start discovering more things from that country,” she says.

	“As people are more open to things from different countries or discover a different genre, like maybe anime, then that opens up a whole world,” she says.
	

	During her early tour to build up Netflix’s hubs, She learned something she found comforting: Every time I’d go in like oh it’s a new country, I’m learning all these things about cultural nuances and a lot of different factors.’ But at the end of the day, it came down to, oh right we support great talent and great voices. That is the same sitting in Hollywood or sitting in another country.”

	***
	
		Beyond ‘Squid Game’	

	10 local-language originals that have resonated globally for Netflix

	Series

	Alice in BorderlandJapan, 2025 (3 seasons)An aimless gamer in Tokyo is thrust into a survival game.

	All of Us Are DeadKorea, 2022 (1 season)High schoolers battle a zombie virus.

	Delhi CrimeIndia, 2019 (3 seasons)Police probe high-profile crimes in the sprawling city.

	LupinFrance, 2021 (Season 4 premieres Oct. 23)A “gentleman thief” works to avenge an injustice inflicted on his father by a wealthy family.

	La PalmaNorway, 2024 (1 season)A Norwegian family struggles to survive a record-breaking tsunami.

	SennaBrazil, 2024 (1 season)The rise and fall of Brazilian Formula 1 driver Ayrton Senna.

	Who Killed Sara?Mexico, 2022 (3 seasons)A wrongly convicted man seeks revenge on the family that framed him.

	Movies

	ExterritorialGermany, 2025An ex-special-forces soldier seeks to free her son after he disappears in the U.S. consulate.

	Society of the SnowSpain, 2024Plane crash victims form unbreakable bonds to survive in the Andes.

	Under ParisFrance, 2024A female scientist battles a killer shark who turns up in the Seine.

title: ‘Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments’: Behind the Scenes of the Satellite of Love
description: In a cozy suburb of Minneapolis, a guy in a blue jumpsuit is once again stuck aboard a space station with his robot pals, watching the worst movies
body:
In a cozy suburb of Minneapolis, a guy in a blue jumpsuit is once again stuck aboard a space station with his robot pals, watching the worst movies ever made.

	To paraphrase the show’s catchy theme song, if you’re wondering how that works, it’s just a TV show, so you should really just relax.

	In May, Variety went behind the scenes of “Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments,” the latest revival of the beloved cult comedy series “Mystery Science Theater 3000,” to get an up close and personal look at how poking fun at bad movies gets done at the highest level.
	

	The series — which features an amiable host and his sharp-tongued sidekicks Tom Servo and Crow riffing on obscure movies like “Manos: The Hands of Fate” and “Space Mutiny” — originally aired from 1988 to 1999, mostly on Comedy Central and the Sci-Fi Channel.


	Joel Hodgson created and starred as that guy forced to screen cheesy flicks; he left mid-run and was replaced by Michael J. Nelson. After the show wrapped, Nelson and fellow “MST3K” writer-stars Kevin Murphy and Bill Corbett took the basic idea and launched their own version, RiffTrax, which started as a website and branched out into live performances and its own FAST channel.

	Then, in 2017, Hodgson revived “MST3K” at Netflix and launched a related streaming platform called The Gizmoplex, but the RiffTrax team wasn’t involved.

	That all changed this year. In January, Hodgson sold his ownership in the series to Radial Entertainment and once again departed. Radial then recruited the RiffTrax team to return for four new episodes. “Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments” was born.
	

	The transition of “MST3K” to Radial allowed the company to approach the RiffTrax team (who hadn’t been formally involved in any new interations of the show since 1999) about joining forces, which they were eager to do. Fans were in: They raised $2.7 million in a Kickstarter campaign to fund the revival, and “The RiffTrax Experiments” were off and running.

	As Variety visits the “MST3K: RiffTrax” set, the cast and crew are nearing the end of a rapid-fire shoot on the new episodes. At this point in the shoot, the host segments that serve as interstitials for the movie mocking that made the original a success have all been filmed. As a result, most of the main sets are already torn down.

	But there are still various robot puppets and spare props lying around the studio, including a sign for the show’s fictional sponsor, ‘Syd’s Olive Loaf.’ There is a definite handmade quality to the props and puppets that are part of the show’s charm.



	

					The Tom Servo and Crow T. Robot puppets, both host segment versions and silhouette versions
	



	“Not to make too much of a social point, but there’s a lot of people getting sick of slop,” Corbett says. “So to know that it is actually physical stuff that was built is kind of a nice thing.”

	Like the original show, “The RiffTrax Experiments” was filmed in Minneapolis, this time at the Cinequipt production facility. Nelson, Murphy, and Corbett return in their original roles both onscreen and behind the camera, while much of the show’s original crew are back as well. That includes director of photography Jeff Stonehouse, props master and puppeteer Patrick Brantseg, and costume designer Beth “Beez” McKeever.

	“I was really proud when we got this thing together and you call people up, and you realize…there’s no baggage,” Nelson says. “It’s not like a band where, “Oh, we don’t talk to that guy anymore.’ It’s just been fun to have everybody back.”

	Also returning to the series are “MST3K” vets Trace Beaulieu and Frank Conniff, both of whom were writers on the original series. Beaulieu also starred as Dr. Clayton Forrester – the mad scientist who initially shot Joel then Mike into space – while Conniff played his sidekick, “TV’s Frank.”



	

					Frank Coniff and Trace Beaulieu as The Mads, TV’s Frank and Dr. Clayton Forrester 
	



	“I’m glad Jeff [Stonehouse] pushed me to do it because it was so much fun,” Beaulieu says. “And then once we were all on set as the Mads, it was just like we hadn’t left.”
	

	“I was overweight and old looking even back then, so there wasn’t much of a much of a change to anything,” Coniff chimes in. Beaulieu laughs and continues, “It just felt very natural. If anything, I wish we could have hung around longer. We should have screwed up more takes, Frank!”

	“I know, our damn professionalism ruined everything,” Conniff adds.

	The shoot is also a family affair. Both Brantseg and Corbett’s daughters worked on the show, while Stonehouse says his son contributed to the design of one of the robot puppets. It’s in keeping with “MST3K’s” legacy of bringing families together for decades now.

	“A very nice lady came up to me once and said, ‘My dad used to watch you!’ Then she had her child with her too,” Corbett says. “So, how many generations are we like pets too? We accept it. We accept our decrepitude.”

	While movie riffing as a comedy form has not taken off to a massive degree, “MST3K” has influenced generations of comedians and performers. “There’s a group in Austin, Texas, called Master Pancake Theater who we’ve worked with, and are really, really good,” Conniff says. “They took what we did and made it their own.”

	The focus of the day is recording riffs for one of the four movies to be featured in the new episodes. While three of the four movies have been revealed — “Sting of Death,” “Space Raiders,” and “Deathsport” — the one being riffed on this particular day is being kept a closely guarded secret.

	For filming the riffs, Nelson, Corbett, and Murphy (and Murphy and Corbett’s puppet characters) take their positions in front of a giant green screen as they do in the show’s trademark silhouette — just like they did in producing the original show.



	

					The set up for filming movie riffs
	



	Concealed behind a cutout made to look like a row of theater seats are the monitors the guys use to watch the movie in real time along with their scripts. It’s incredibly precise, with jokes timed out to the second to match what’s happening in the movie.



	

					A closer look at how movie riffs are filmed
	



	Keeping a watchful eye over the shoot from a balcony above the soundstage floor are Sean Thomason and Conor Lastowka, RiffTrax’s longtime senior writers and producers. They follow along with the script, making sure everything matches up.
	

	On how writing for RiffTrax differs from “MST3K,” Lastowka says, “There’s no comparison. It’s a very different rhythm writing for this show. The bots & Mike are characters, but at RiffTrax Mike, Kevin and Bill are just themselves, so we can make references to their lives in a way we can’t for Mike, Servo and Crow.”

	“Bill and Kevin are like Little Rascals as the bots, and then Mike reins them in,” Thomason adds. “It’s very much that big brother dynamic.”



	

					Sean Thomason and Conow Lastowka watching over filming
	



	While all involved say that movie riffing is not an art form for all writers, it is nevertheless incredibly efficient once shooting begins. Given that you can’t really see the actors’ mouths moving, if they happen to flub a line, they can quickly re-record and dub it in later. The team starts shooting around 9:30 a.m. and wrap up for the day by 2 p.m.

	Still, it’s a big change from doing RiffTrax as the three main stars have been doing for the past 20 years.

	“RiffTrax is audio-based,” Murphy says. “So we have a studio at our homes. We can start and stop. We don’t have the same sort of performance aspect to it. This is more akin to when we do live shows, where we really have to be on and have to have everything buttoned down before we get out there.”

	But recording the riffs is the end of a long process of watching bad movies — a regimen that few would recommend, including the stars of the show.

	“You’re watching the same movie, chunks of it at least, over and over and over again. It’s almost like a close reading of a text, you just dive into it so much, it’s really bad. It’s probably not mentally healthy,” Murphy jokes.



	

					Series stars Michael J. Nelson, Bill Corbett, and Kevin Murphy
	



	“Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments — Sting of Death” is now available at the RiffTrax website. The remaining three episodes will debut in the coming weeks.

schema.headline: ‘Mystery Science Theater 3000: The RiffTrax Experiments’: Behind the Scenes of the Satellite of Love

title: Jeissy Trompiz’s ‘Three Houses’ Explores a Venezuela Where Afro and Indigenous Communities Sit on the ‘Periphery of the Periphery’
description:
“I don’t know what to tell you.”

	For a time, that was Jeissy Trompiz’s answer when his Brazilian filmmaker friend would ask him about Venezuela.
body:
“I don’t know what to tell you.”

	For a time, that was Jeissy Trompiz’s answer when his Brazilian filmmaker friend would ask him about Venezuela.

	Trompiz left Maracaibo, the oil city where he grew up, in 2014 to study filmmaking at the International School of Film and TV in Cuba, just before Venezuela’s economic and political crisis deepened.


	He later completed a residency in Italy, made short films in Cuba and Indonesia, and settled in the Dominican Republic in 2019, where he now lives and works. The pandemic and passport renewal problems kept him away from Venezuela for about six years.
	

	When he finally returned home, he was confronted with a changed country he had struggled to explain — even to himself.

	“The situation was really sad and shocking,” he told Variety. He couldn’t shake the comparison to Cuba, another country in crisis.

	“When I went back to Venezuela, I started to think: Now I can tell you.”

	So he started filming “Three Houses” (“Tres casas”), a documentary that takes the form of a video letter from Maracaibo to his friend. Trompiz describes making it as a form of “therapy.”

	The film is among the projects selected for the Vancouver Film Festival’s newly launched Business Hub Works-In-Progress Forum.

	There’s a sense of urgency for Trompiz to tell this story — even though he’s already been working on it for four years. He initially shot on the streets with a mobile phone, but his mother worried about his safety. She had been involved in promoting the opposition movement, had seen friends jailed, been a target of accusations and pushed out of a public job. Local mafias and extortion posed another threat.
	

	“I couldn’t shoot with my camera in the street anymore, because my mom was afraid to be extorted.” The film moved indoors. Three family homes. Just ordinary people, collecting modest salaries, dealing with the pressures of daily life in Venezuela under its government.

	Trompiz’s mother features prominently. After he showed her a cut and asked if she wanted to continue, she told him: “If you believe that it will help the political situation in Venezuela in any way, if it at least helps in this process of trying to look for a democracy in Venezuela — do it. Do not be afraid for me.”

	They also created a plan should anything go wrong. “Those are the kinds of conversations [you have].”

	Trompiz, who is Afro Indigenous, grew up on the edge of Maracaibo and sees the community he is capturing as existing on a kind of periphery — not simply geographically, but politically and culturally.

	Caracas is what much of the outside world pictures when it thinks of Venezuela, he told Variety. The arts, he argues, need to rethink their inclusion of other places “because those are different points of view that can create a more complex perception, analytical situation, and narrative.”

	Afro and Indigenous communities, he says, sit in the “periphery of the periphery.”

	The country’s rapidly changing political situation has repeatedly forced him to reshape the film. “All of us filmmakers, we are always reshaping and rewriting the film,” he says. “The film by itself finds the way to survive.”

	Although many of his friends and family celebrated Nicolás Maduro’s removal, Trompiz could not bring himself to do so.

	“I don’t want to thank Trump for this. I wanted Maduro out, but not with U.S. intervention, because it won’t be free.”

	The root of fascism, he says, is still in Caracas. He says that now people are really angry and sad.

	He acknowledges that he’s seen a few changes for the better. He’s less worried that his mother would be jailed; there’s somewhat more criticism of the government on television (though, curiously, no U.S. criticism); some opposition figures have been released and small protests are possible. But he says that the changes haven’t been significant — there are still people in jail for posting critical content on social media over the past few years — and economic conditions have worsened.
	

	“It’s a terrible situation, because it’s like a two-headed political government. Trump and this other government from Venezuela.”

	Millions have left the country, leaving those who remain uncertain about what comes next.

	Trompiz’s film isn’t meant to criticize a particular government or boost the opposition. Rather, he wants to show how easily governments can become fascist and oppressive. And what that does to ordinary people.

	“Even a left-side government can be fascist,” he says. But with U.S. intervention, “we can see that a left or right [leaning] government can not only be fascist, but can also become allies” when there’s an economic or political deal to be had.

	Working on the film has also taken an emotional toll.

	“It’s worse than therapy,” Trompiz says, describing the rollercoaster of emotions he experienced while editing. “I cried when I hadn’t cried before.”

	“When I was in Venezuela, I was trying to feel stronger. A part of me was proud, saying, ‘I don’t want to cry for this government, or for this oppression.’ But when I started to work on this film, I started to cry. I got sad, and I got angry, and then the reflection starts again. What can I do? And the film also is part of the reflection.”

	“Three Houses” is produced by Alamar Films (Venezuela), Piso Tres (Dominican Republic) and Peixe Aranha (Portugal), with support from the Doha Film Institute and Eurodoc Caribe.

schema.headline: Jeissy Trompiz’s ‘Three Houses’ Explores a Venezuela Where Afro and Indigenous Communities Sit on the ‘Periphery of the Periphery’

title: ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’
description: It was a “helluva” time at New York City Comic-Con, where an audience remember interrupted the “Helluva Boss” panel by repeatedly shouting over the
body:
It was a “helluva” time at New York City Comic-Con, where an audience remember interrupted the “Helluva Boss” panel by repeatedly shouting over the cast.

	Following multiple attempts to silence the heckling, actor Brandon Rogers seemingly threatened the fan in a video posted online.

	“You need to shut the fuck up right now,” Rogers said during the panel. “I’m going to jump over this fence and end you. It’s not cute.”
	

	The fan continued to shout, which prompted the actor to get out of his seat and approach the audience, saying, “You need to get the fuck out right now, or I will make you leave.”


	When nobody on the NYCC staff stepped in, Rogers asked, “Isn’t there someone in a vest? Bulletproof one, maybe?” After a bit of silence, he added, “Is anyone working this fucking event? Can someone please get this motherfucker the hell out of here? I swear to God.”

	In a statement to Variety, a spokesperson for ReedPop wrote, “We are aware of a repeated disturbance from a fan in the audience during Thursday’s ‘Helluva Boss’ panel. While the situation was addressed after the panel, action was not taken swiftly enough, and we apologize to the panelists, moderator, and fans in attendance for the disruption. We are taking steps to ensure any future incidents are addressed in a swifter manner.”

	The panel also featured Vivian Nichole Nixon, Erica Lindbeck, Bryce Pinkham, Harvey Guillén, Vivienne Medrano, Richard Steven Horvitz and Perri Nemiroff to discuss the animated series, which Rogers wrote and developed.

schema.headline: ‘Helluva Boss’ Actor Lashes Out at NYCC Heckler: ‘I’m Going to Jump Over This Fence and End You’

title: Music Industry Moves: Believe Names Adriana Sein President of Americas; Guy Moot Joins NMPA Board
description: France-based music company Believe has named Adriana Sein to the newly created role of President, Americas. She will lead Believe’s commercial opera
body:
France-based music company Believe has named Adriana Sein to the newly created role of President, Americas. She will lead Believe’s commercial operations across North and South America, overseeing the Label & Artist Solutions business lines and driving the company’s continued expansion across the Americas, including the U.S., Canada and Latin America. She will report to Believe’s Global Head of Music, Romain Vivien.

	Sein most recently served as Senior Vice President & Global Head of Artist & Market Development at ADA Music, WMG’s global independent music distribution and artist services arm, where she led the distribution business in EMEA and Latin America, global marketing and client partnerships, and spearheaded ADA’s new market expansion efforts via integrations and partnerships in MENA and Africa. Previously, she held senior roles at Columbia and Ultra Records.
	

	“Adriana is a successful senior executive leader with a super strong track record in the global music industry,” Vivien said. “Her multiple market expertise and deep understanding of both distribution and artist development businesses added to a solid strategic vision make her the best person to hone our operations, increase our impact, and continue growing our business throughout the Americas. Adriana joining Believe stands as a testament to our continued investment in the region, particularly in the United States, and our commitment to help develop creators, labels and artists with best in class services, expertise, and leadership.


	+ Guy Moot, CEO and recently named sole chairman of Warner Chappell Music publishing, has joined the National Music Publishers Association’s Board of Directors.
	

	“Guy Moot is one of the most distinguished creative and business minds in music,” said NMPA president-CEO David Israelite. “From legends to emerging talent, he has a track record of identifying and championing incredible songwriters. The NMPA Board will benefit greatly from his perspective and expertise after over 30 innovative years in the industry.”

	+ Empire Publishing has made a strong move into the Latin music world by bringing in Emilio Morales as SVP, Business Development for Latin America. Based in Puerto Rico, Morales comes to Empire after a run as Managing Director of Rimas Publishing, the independent San Juan powerhouse behind the catalogs of Bad Bunny, Eladio Carrión, Mora, Subelo Neo and more. He unified its three companies under the Rimas Publishing brand and grew the roster to more than 150 writers and producers across Puerto Rico, Mexico, Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and more. He also launched Rimas Publishing Girls, an initiative spotlighting women producers and composers in trap and reggaeton, along with a wellbeing program for the company’s creators.

	“Emilio has spent his career proving what’s possible when you invest in songwriters and producers and give them the tools to win and his proven success in Latin America makes him the perfect fit to lead our expansion across the region,” said Ghazi, CEO and founder of Empire.

	+ Sony Music Publishing U.K., alongside JV partner One Two Many Songs, have announced a worldwide extension of their exclusive publishing agreement with Grammy and Ivor Novello-nominated and Mercury Prize-winning songwriter-producer Gianluca Buccellati, which includes all catalogue and future works.

	Buccellati has worked extensively with the Marias, cowriting and coproducing their hit “No One Noticed” as well as singer Maria Zardoya’s solo project Not for Radio, and also collaborated extensively with Arlo Parks on her debut “Collapsed in Sunbeams,” Declan McKenna, Paris Texas, Biig Piig, Danielle Ponder, Tei Shi and Cailin Russo.

	Buccellati said, “It was a no brainer to extend my working relationship with OTM and Sony. Alex, Felix and the team I’ve nurtured a relationship with through my first term feel like family.”

	+ Kenyan singer-songwriter Bien has pacgted with a joint venture between Quality Control and Courtesy Of, marking Quality Control’s first African artist. The first release under the deal is “I’ll Be Okay,” the first single from Bien’s forthcoming album.
	

	“Bien has it!,” enthused QC co-founder Pierre “P” Thomas. “He’s got the songs, a great performer, strong fan base, and he’s already done a lot on his own. For me, it’s about how much bigger we can expand his global reach. There’s a great opportunity here to work alongside Tek to bring their vision to life, and that’s what excites me.”

	+ The music-creation platform Splice has named Kate Guarente-Smith Head of Communications at the company. Guarente-Smith will oversee overall communications strategy across the Splice platform, including Sounds, Instrument, Spitfire Audio and Kits AI, as well as the company’s strategic partnerships with industry leaders and artists. Previously, she held early leadership roles at GitHub and Slack.

	“Kate has a track record of building comms programs that bring diverse audiences into the fold, and helping people see what’s possible for them as technology evolves. I experienced this first-hand during our time together at GitHub,” said Kakul Srivastava, CEO at Splice.

	Tuesday, October 6

	Country star Thomas Rhett and Hybe Americas’ Nashville-based label Blue Highway Records have announced a new partnership, Fifty-One/Forty-Nine Records. Described as “artist-led,” the partnership offers “an innovative approach to the artist-label relationship,” according to the announcement. following more than a decade of shared success. (Pictured above, L-R: Blue Highway CEO Jake Basden, Rhett and G Major Mgmt’s Virginia Bunetta.)

	“When we started talking about what the next chapter could look like, I knew I didn’t simply want to make another deal. I wanted to build something that reflected the legacy and shaped the future of my music,” Rhett said. “From my initial conversations with Jake and the leadership team at Blue Highway, it was clear they, too, were thinking differently about what a record company can be for an artist today. This allows me the opportunity to own the body of work I’ve spent my entire career creating, while still having an ambitious team and global infrastructure around me for my future recordings.”

	Blue Highway CEO Jake Basden said, “Thomas Rhett has always been an artist, a songwriter, a performer who brings the best of what being a progressive country artist is today: someone who is willing to explore how other genres merge with Nashville without losing his roots, without sounding calculated or forced. Having watched Thomas Rhett come into his own and then achieve major success, I am honored to be his partner going forward.”
	

	+ Grammy and Latin Grammy-winning Puerto Rican rapper-producer Wisin has signed with WME for representation in all areas. 

	The move comes a month after the September launch of “La Universidad del Perreo,” his new 12-track album and six months after his guest appearance with Karol G at Coachella. Over the years he has also collaborated with Daddy Yankee, Jennifer Lopez, Pitbull, J Balvin, Ricky Martin, Maluma, Rosalía, and more. Wisin is managed by Chris Duque of D27 Entertainment.

	+ Willard Ahdritz, founder of Kobalt Music Group, has launched Ahdritz Capital Partners, a music and media technology investment firm, and announced that Isabel Keulen, most recently CEO of SSE Ventures and SSE Business, has joined as an investment partner, based in Stockholm and working in association with the New York-based Ahdritz and investment partner Stephen Langer.

	Ahdritz founded Kobalt in 2000 and led it for more than two decades as CEO and then chairman, building one of the largest independent music companies in the world. He also co-founded the digital collection society AMRA. Ahdritz stepped down from Kobalt when it was acquired by Primary Wave in July 2026.“Music is global, yet the capital and networks founders need have been concentrated in a few cities,” said Ahdritz. “We want to support founders and innovation not only in those markets, but also in other parts of the world too.”

	+ Artist House, the independent label-publisher-management-studio company founded by Grammy-winning songwriter-producer Gregg Wattenberg and Steve Lerner, has named Jim Cooperman chief operating officer. He will oversee business and legal affairs, operations and publishing for the New York-based music company.

	Cooperman joins after 14 years at Madison Square Garden Entertainment, where he served as SVP and associate general counsel of legal and business affairs and played a key role in structuring deals for events at Sphere in Las Vegas, including residencies by U2, Phish, Dead & Company and the Eagles. Previously, he held senior roles at Wind-up Entertainment, BMG, RED, Relativity, Loud and RCA Records.

	“I’ve had the privilege of working alongside Jim over the years, and I’m thrilled that he has joined the Artist House team,” said Lerner. “We’ve created something meaningful in a remarkably short time, and Jim’s talent, experience, and integrity will be an important part of our continued growth.”
	

	+ Los Angeles-based band Lo Moon has signed with Easy Does It Records and [PIAS] and will release their first single for the label on Wednesday, “Satellite.” The track was written by frontman Matt Lowell and produced by Alex Farrar (MJ Lenderman, Hotline TNT, Wednesday); the band recently completed dates supporting the War on Drugs.

	+ Floating Leaf Entertainment, the artist management company founded by Jeb Hurt based in Austin, Texas, has joined Red Light Management, bringing its roster — including multi-platinum artist Koe Wetzel, Kolby Cooper, Fox & Vead and others — into the management company founded by Coran Capshaw.“This is about taking what we’ve built at Floating Leaf and giving it an even bigger runway,” said Hurt. “We’ve always been incredibly focused on the artist — who they are, what makes them different and how we can help build a career around that. Red Light has an incredible history of doing the same thing at a global level.”“Jeb has built something special at Floating Leaf,” said Ben Kline of Red Light Management. “He has an incredible instinct for artists and has earned the kind of trust that you can’t manufacture. Koe, Kolby, Fox & Vead and the rest of the roster are a reflection of that.”

	+ The Beggars Group of Labels (4AD, Matador Records, Rough Trade Records, XL Recordings and Young) has added four new staff members and a brand-new department: Max Datner, Ariana Mamnoon, Rrita Hashani and Molly McGuffin. Datner and Mamnoon will comprise the radio and music discovery department, while Hashani and McGuffin join the marketing team.

	The announcement reads, “As phrases like ‘marketing’ and ‘radio’ have evolved over the last couple of years, we have found it beneficial to redefine what those kinds of roles mean for us in today’s music industry. As we embark on massive album campaigns for Queens of the Stone Age, Erykah Badu, Fontaines D.C., Julia Jacklin and more, this is the perfect time to expand with new roles that dedicated to identifying modern and creative ways to champion both established and new artists.”

	+ Warner Music Group has announced an expansion of its Middle East and North Africa (MENA) leadership: Ahmed Nureni has been promoted to Managing Director, MENA, reporting to President of EMEA, Recorded Music, Guillermo Gonzalez; while Ahmad Alghawanmeh joins the company as General Manager, MENA, reporting directly to Nureni.
	

	Nureni will oversee Warner Music’s MENA’s overarching vision, corporate development, strategic joint ventures, and catalog expansion across all markets. Alghawanmeh joins WMG from Sony Music Entertainment and will lead commercial growth, business development, market expansion initiatives, and multi-territory operational delivery for the region.

	Gonzalez said, “MENA continues to be one of the fastest-growing music markets in the world, and Warner Music is committed to staying at the forefront of that momentum. Ahmed has done an outstanding job building our presence in the region over the last several years, and will develop this further in his new role, while, in Ahmad we are adding an executive with sharp commercial instincts, deep regional relationships, and a proven track record in digital strategy.”

	+ Activist Artists Management has announced the addition of Chelsea Fodero and Mak Symmonds as Artist Managers. Most recently, Fodero served as Day-to-Day Manager for Usher, helping to oversee his “Past Present Future” World Tour, as well as creative, styling, merchandising and brand partnerships. She previously managed Grammy-winning Producer of the Year Andrew Watt.

	Symmonds was most director of marketing at Smack, leading strategy across the company’s management, label and publishing divisions. There, she worked closely with Grammy-winning songwriter and founder Shane McAnally, as well as Walker Hayes and actress and singer Jenna Davis. Previously, she served as day-to-day manager Chris Tomlin, Patrick Droney and Redferrin. Fodero is based in New York, while Symmonds is based in Nashville and Los Angeles; the company’s roster includes the Lumineers, Orville Peck, Dwight Yoakam, the Grateful Dead, Dead & Company (co-managed with Azoff/Moir), the Pretty Reckless and Young the Giant, among others. 

	+ Vibee, the music-led destination experience company founded by Live Nation, today announced three promotions across its marketing team. Dave Johnston has been promoted from Senior Marketing Manager to Associate Director, Marketing; Merisanda Finely from Digital Marketing Specialist to Digital Marketing Manager; and Lory Hagopian from Senior Designer to Lead Creative/Brand Designer. All three will continue to report to Doneen Lombardi, VP/Head of Marketing.
	

	“As Vibee continues to grow, so does the incredible marketing team responsible for bringing our packages and immersive experiences to life and getting them in front of music fans around the world,” Lombardi said. “Dave, Merisanda and Lory have each made meaningful contributions to our valuable partnerships and overall business.”

title: Air Supply Rocks on With World Tours, a New Album and a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame: ‘The Term Soft Rock Makes Me Sick’
description: When it comes to Russell Hitchcock and Graham Russell — partners behind the 50-year-plus hit machine Air Supply — the only four-letter word in their
body: When it comes to Russell Hitchcock and Graham Russell — partners behind the 50-year-plus hit machine Air Supply — the only four-letter word in their vocabulary is “soft.”Sure, British-born songwriter-harmonist Russell and Australian vocalist Hitchcock sing luscious love songs like “Every Woman in the World” and “Even the Nights Are Better” and make mellow top 10 albums like “The One That You Love” — to the tune of 100 million records sold worldwide — “but you can’t call it ‘soft,’” says Russell, calling from Los Angeles just hours before another of Air Supply’s concerts (more than 6,000 since the duo launched in 1975). “When we play live, we rock. LOUD.”Hitchcock chimes in on how energetic Air Supply’s shows have been forever — they played with AC/DC in the 1970s — and of the rough tones of Stones-y new tracks like “I Want Your Love” and “Son of the Father.” The vocalist then makes a proclamation: “I fancy calling what Air Supply does ‘romantic rock and roll.’ The term soft rock makes me sick.”Done. Air Supply creates romantic rock and roll filled with the passion of their youth, for the love of their devoted fanbase, the Airheads, and to follow the muse they were gifted with since the 1970s.Media tracking databases WhatSong and Tunefind credit Air Supply with 64-plus serene sync placements since 1979’s smash “Lost in Love.” They have a new album, due out soon, “A Matter of Time,” a biopic in development and received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame Oct. 8, which cemented their legacy as hitmakers and an enduring touring band.“This might sound cliché, but we really do do this for our fans — better shows, better performances,” Russell says adamantly. “That’s our driving force. When we decided to form Air Supply, we really didn’t know what we were doing. I’m not a particularly great musician. But together we created this bond from the start.”Hitchcock reminds Variety that when it came to building Air Supply, “There were no grand plans or future projections. We just wanted to do it,” before Russell finishes his partner’s sentiment.“Fifty-one years later, we have the same incentive: we just want to do it. And to continue to do it at such a high level as we do is a gift from somewhere. We love that gift. We’re guided by that.”That gift started when “the two Russells” met as part of the vocal chorus of 1975’s Australian production of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Jesus Christ Superstar.”“My recollection of Graham during the first rehearsal, learning our choreography — we can’t dance, I can tell you — was that he fell and sprained his ankle,” says Hitchcock, as both men laugh. “THAT made him stand out. Plus, he’s 6’ 4”. Once we started talking, though, we had so much in common. Both saw the Beatles, independently, in London and Australia. We weren’t part of the theater kids who thought they were better than everybody else. Our birthdays are three days apart. We’re both working-class guys who grew up without brothers. We were that production’s black sheep — all of which drew us close to each other. Then I heard him playing guitar off to the side of the stage, one of his own songs. That sealed the deal. I never met anyone who played their own songs. We started singing together that day.”Russell adds that Hitchcock “was the one who took me to get my ankle taken care of that day.”Not only did Air Supply start dropping albums (like their self-titled debut in 1976) guitarist Russell states, “Our first single, ‘Love and Other Bruises,’ actually came out while we were still in ‘Jesus Christ Superstar,’ but we couldn’t tell anyone as that was against our contractual obligations. It was a massive hit in Australia, too, but we had to hide that.”But despite releasing additional albums and winning Aussie gold records, Air Supply struggled. “We got put in front of the lions quickly, and for some time,” says Russell.Then Rod Stewart asked them to open his 1977 U.S. tour, and “Lost in Love” caught the attention of then-Arista label head Clive Davis.“I knew the moment I heard ‘Lost in Love,’ it was IT,” stresses Hitchcock.“But we were still going nowhere when we released it,” says Russell. “It was a hit in Australia, but we still made $200 a night.”Unbeknownst to the Air pair at the time, however, Arista picked up an option on “Lost in Love,” and pushed the single into the U.S. charts. “I called Arista, charges reversed, and got through to Clive, who told me to start writing more songs as Air Supply was about to have the biggest hit of the year.”Clive Davis being Clive Davis, he added background singers and edited the run time.“No songwriter wants that,” says Russell. “[But] once Clive got involved, and we made him part of our circle, we knew it would be OK — that’s how we became us.”“We didn’t have a choice,” Hitchcock says laughing, about the “Lost in Love” changes, Davis’ lyrical fixes and non-Air Supply-written songs that Davis brought to them from Jim Steinman (“Making Love Out of Nothing at All”) and Ken Bell & Co. (“Even the Nights Are Better”). “Clive was feared and revered at the same time, and deserves nothing but gratitude from us,” he adds.But calling their own shots brought Air Supply to where they are now — such as last year’s sold-out Carnegie Hall show and a new album with rougher edges, which may be their final recorded effort.“Thinking this might be our last album gave me license to do what I wanted without having to worry about hit singles,” says Russell. “We wanted to have fun. If we do go out after this one, we’re happy.”Hitchcock reminds us that, after 51 years, he’s still amazed and inspired by “Russell being a guy who writes every day — always playing guitar, never without something to record what he’s doing.”Russell admires Hitchcock’s frontman abilities. “He’s the one in the spotlight,” says the songwriter of the singer. “That’s what Russell does best — be that lead person. It takes a lot of balls to do what Russell does. Can you say ‘balls’ in an interview? Anyway, that’s why Air Supply works. We allow ourselves to both do what we love to do. What we’re good at. It’s cool.”Going back to Russell’s ‘last album’ sentiment, Hitchcock faces facts. “Look, our last album before ‘A Matter of Time’ was 16 years ago (‘Mumbo Jumbo’). If we wait another 15, 16 years, I’ll be 94.”“Every artist makes a last album,” says Russell, with a hint of black humor. “Maybe we could call the next one ‘One Foot in the Grave.’”Putting aside the gallows humor, the duo reflect on their Walk of Fame star.“Along with waiting for a songwriting Grammy for Graham — tragedy if that doesn’t happen before he croaks — getting this Walk of Fame star is great validation,” says Hitchcock. “It’s hard to comprehend being so enshrined. Wait, that sounds as if we’re being embalmed.”Russell adds, laughing, “There’s that ‘One Foot in the Grave’ thing. All I can say is that when I heard we were getting our star, I burst into tears. It’s just incredible.”

schema.headline: Air Supply Rocks on With World Tours, a New Album and a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame: ‘The Term Soft Rock Makes Me Sick’

title: Sadie Sink in Talks to Star in The Guest,’ Based on Emma Cline’s Bestseller
description: Newly-minted MCU star and “Stranger Things” alum Sadie Sink is in talks to star in and produce “The Guest,” a feature adaptation of Emma Cline’s bes
body:
Newly-minted MCU star and “Stranger Things” alum Sadie Sink is in talks to star in and produce “The Guest,” a feature adaptation of Emma Cline’s bestselling 2024 novel.

	A24 and Square Peg are in negotiations to adapt Cline’s novel — which follows as “a calculating grifter navigates the treacherous world of Summer in the Hamptons” — with writer-director Lorene Scafaria (“Hustlers,” “Succession”) in talks to helm the project.
	

	Published in 2024 by Penguin Random House, “The Guest” was longlisted for the Pen/Faulkner award, as well as named a Belletrist Book Club pick and best book of the year by more than a dozen publications, including The New Yorker, Time, NPR and The Washington Post.


	News of the project comes as Sink graduated from the supernatural world of Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” to join the Marvel Cinematic Universe as the ultrapowerful mutant Jean Grey in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which became the highest-grossing film in domestic box office history after swinging into theaters in July. Sink also delivered standout performances in the Oscar-winning film “The Whale,” the recent West End production of “Romeo and Juliet” and a Tony-nominated turn in Broadway’s “John Proctor is the Villain.” She will next star in Marvel’s “X-Men” reboot, directed by Jake Schreier and set to release on May 5, 2028.

	In addition to 2019’s “Hustlers,” Scafaria wrote and directed “Seeking a Friend for the End of the World” and “The Meddler,” and wrote the adapted screenplay for “Nick & Norah’s Infinite Playlist.” Scafaria’s TV work includes directing episodes of “New Girl” and “Succession,” the latter for which she was nominated for a DGA Award and a Primetime Emmy. Currently, Scafaria serves as executive producer and a director on HBO’s “I Love LA.”
	

	Sink is represented by WME, Peikoff Mahan and imPRint; and Scafaria is repped by UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern.

	Deadline first reported news of the developing project.

schema.headline: Sadie Sink in Talks to Star in The Guest,’ Based on Emma Cline’s Bestseller

title: Raindance Film Festival Exec Director David Martinez Steps Down (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Raindance Film Festival executive director David Martinez has stepped down from his post after more than a decade with the organization.

	Martinez
body:
Raindance Film Festival executive director David Martinez has stepped down from his post after more than a decade with the organization.

	Martinez joined Raindance in 2012 as the festival producer and programmer for Latam territories before his appointment as executive director five years ago.

	“I stepped into leadership at Raindance because I believe passionately in the power of independent film to challenge, inspire and connect people. My aim was always to support filmmakers and broaden our international scope. I am incredibly proud of the achievements we made during my time at Raindance, with immense gratitude to the partners who believed in our cause, the entire team at Raindance— and, above all, the filmmakers and audiences who make Raindance what it is now,” he said.
	

	During his tenure, Martinez significantly expanded Raindance’s international reach, establishing new programs and partnerships with filmmakers and industry partners across Mexico, Chile, Catalonia, Cyprus, Germany and beyond. Audience attendance doubled compared to previous years.


	He also broadened the festival’s industry and professional development activities, launching the House of Raindance, Raindance XR, the Raindance Script Competition and its LGBTQ+ strand, as well as the Cannes Villa Party, while strengthening strategic sponsorships and partnerships and elevating Raindance’s global profile and support for filmmakers.

	Said Raindance founder Elliot Grove: “David has been instrumental in Raindance’s evolution over the past decade. His passion for independent cinema, his advocacy for filmmakers and his collaborative leadership have broadened Raindance’s outlook and left the festival in a strong position for the future.”
	

	About his plans for the future, Martinez told Variety: “I will carry on championing independent filmmakers through my new agency, Casa Leo PR, sharing the expertise needed to navigate the film festival circuit and awards season, while also continuing my work as an awards consultant at London Flair PR.”

	Martinez and former Raindance producer Jacky Orozco launched the boutique festival agency Casa Leo PR just this year. Among its first campaigns were with Netflix on the London screening of Maite Alberdi’s “A Child of My Own” and support for Humberto Busto on his Venice Biennale College title “Tijuana todavía.” It is representing Mexico’s Santiago Maza (“State of Silence”) and his latest work, the documentary short “Black Shine” (“El brillo negro”), which world premieres at the upcoming Morelia Film Festival in Mexico.

	Short follows the families of the 65 miners killed in the 2006 Pasta de Conchos disaster as they fight, decades later, to recover their loved ones. Through their grief and persistence, the film explores memory, resistance and a wound left open by institutional neglect.

	The 24th Morelia Film Festival runs Oct. 16–25.

schema.headline: Raindance Film Festival Exec Director David Martinez Steps Down (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Channing Dungey Extends Deal at Skydance As Head of Warner Bros. TV Group and U.S. Networks
description: No surprise here: With Channing Dungey opting to remain with Warner Bros. TV Group, she is believed to have sealed a deal with its new parent compan
body:
No surprise here: With Channing Dungey opting to remain with Warner Bros. TV Group, she is believed to have sealed a deal with its new parent company, Skydance. Terms or length of the new contract aren’t known, but obviously with the new company structure and expanded role for Dungey, a revised employment agreement would come with the changes.

	As previously reported, Dungey will continue to oversee Warner Bros. TV Group, but there’s no word yet on any title change. (She’s currently chairman, although not using the “CEO” part of her title right now post-merger.) Dungey also continues to oversee U.S. Networks — and under the merger, Dungey will now be charged with the Paramount Media Networks stable of cablers in addition to her ongoing role as head of Warner Bros. Discovery’s channels.
	

	Dungey joins other former Warner Bros. Discovery execs like Casey Bloys (now co-chair and chief content officer for Skydance DTC) and JB Perrette (now co-chair & chief business officer, Skydance TV and co-chair & chief business officer, Skydance DTC) in also reupping with the new company under new terms.


	In a memo Dungey sent to staffers earlier this week, she confirmed that she’ll be reporting to Perrette (in his Skydance TV role) and newly named Skydance TV co-chair and chief content officer George Cheeks.

	Cheeks and Perrette are expected to reveal the Skydance TV executive structure next week, including perhaps new titles for execs like Dungey, CBS Studios president David Stapf and Paramount TV Studios president Matt Thunell. 

	In her note, Dungey noted the studio’s recent successes, including 13 new series orders and 13 series renewals so far this year and its overall slate of more than 80 titles for over 20 platforms.
	

	And in a conversation with Variety earlier this summer, she expressed her interest in sticking with the company post-merger: “I love my team at Warner Bros. Television Group. I love our shows, our talent. And I’ve become very happy in my U.S. networks role, which was something that I didn’t see coming almost two years ago. The best-case scenario for me is something that allows me to continue to play around in both of these spaces.”

schema.headline: Channing Dungey Extends Deal at Skydance As Head of Warner Bros. TV Group and U.S. Networks

title: Woah Vicky Says Her Mom Has Been Missing For Two Weeks
description:
Woah Vicky
                          My Mom Is Missing
body:
Woah Vicky
                          My Mom Is Missing
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 9, 2026
                            8:53 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 9, 2026
                                9:41 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Woah Vicky says her mom, Carla, has been missing for weeks ... she's asking the public for any information they may have ... and cops are investigating.
      
    
            The influencer shared a missing poster with a photo of herself and her mom ... claiming her family hasn't heard from Carla in about two weeks.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            It sounds like Carla vanished after recently traveling by bus from Atlanta to Miami to see Vicky ... and the family is "urgently seeking information" regarding her whereabouts and safety.
      

            It's so serious, in fact, that a note on the missing poster instructs anyone with information to call the cops ASAP.
      
    
            Police in Miami tell TMZ ... a missing person's report was generated Thursday night and cops are investigating.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Vicky also said she "went to jail for fighting with my mom" in Florida two weeks ago, and when she got out of custody, she couldn't get in contact with her mom. She says her mother's phone appears to be off.
      
    
            TMZ confirmed Vicky was arrested on a misdemeanor battery charge in Miami on Sept. 25 after cops were called for a report of a woman claiming she had been assaulted by her daughter and needed help retrieving her belongings.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            According to the police report, obtained by TMZ, the woman claimed she was staying with her daughter for 5 days while visiting, and her daughter assaulted her by placing her hands around her neck. Cops say Vicky told them there was an argument but denied assaulting her mother.
      
    
            Police say they saw bruises on the alleged victim's arms.
      
    
            We've reached out to Vicky ... so far, no word back.

description:
'Journey' Drummer
                          Deen Castronovo Rushed To Hospital
body:
'Journey' Drummer
                          Deen Castronovo Rushed To Hospital
                          ... After Medical Scare During Show
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 9, 2026
                            5:37 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Legendary rock band Journey had to hit the pause button on their Oklahoma concert Thursday night -- after their drummer suffered a medical scare onstage and was rushed to the hospital.
      
    
            Deen Castronovo fell ill two songs into their set at BOK Center in Tulsa, stopping the show in its tracks during their 2026 "Final Frontier" tour.
      
    
            Shortly after Castronovo left the stage, keyboardist Jonathan Cain walked up to the microphone and told the packed crowd that Deen had a medical emergency.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Video posted online shows Cain explaining to the audience that it's an "unfortunate situation," while apologizing for the inconvenience. Cain also asked everyone to keep Castronovo in their prayers.
      
    
            Minutes later, guitarist Neal Schon came back onstage to report that Castronovo had been rushed to a hospital. Schon also said Castronovo would be replaced by his drum tech, Steve Toomey, for the rest of the show.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The rest of the band then returned to the stage with singer Arnel Pineda also asking for prayers for Castronovo before they dove back into their set.
      
    
            As for Castronovo's condition, Schon said the drummer is going to be "fine" at one point during the concert.
      
    
            And the band got to the finish line without another hitch. What a journey!!!

title: Cornell Jane Doe Texted With Frat Bro Matthew Ingalls About Campus Rumors, Sex
body:
Jane Doe was in investigation mode in the days and weeks after the alleged sexual assault, working with one of the men she would later accuse of rape to find out who was spreading rumors about the sexual encounter.
      
    
            TMZ obtained a text chain between Matthew Ingalls and Jane Doe. On October 23 -- four days after the frat party -- she tells him, "bro everyone knows✌️i'm incredibly stressed out."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Matthew responds ... "Dude I have no f***ing idea, this s*** is incredibly frustrating and I know how fast nonsense spreads at this school. It's fan behavior from everyone talking about it. Boring people who have nothing to do with their time."
      

            Jane says the rumors are "f***ing RUINING my life temporarily. my reputation is destroyed and i'm utterly ashamed. i'm f***ing pissed because this many people shouldn't know and i feel like i know who some of the rats in the room were."
      
    
            She adds ... "literally people are making it crazier every f***ing day."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Matthew consoles her after she mentions having a UTI, and says of the rumors, "Stupid bitches like to yap, and the fact they're doing it shows that they're jealous of you for any number of reasons."
      
    
            He says she has nothing to be ashamed of and tells her, "The only shameful thing is how this spread and how much people won't shut up about it - which just reflects poorly on them tbh."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Jane agrees people on campus are "jealous" of them, then gets philosophical about sex.
      
    
            She writes ... "but also like everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and s**t is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common,, i'm also really open minded tho."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            TMZ broke the story ... in a separate text chain with Jonathan Newell, another Cornell frat bro named in her suit, Jane mentioned a three-way with him and Matthew. She said she liked being with them and said "i don't think we should feel any shame for the part. our body our choice asf."
      
    
            Jane and Matthew text for several more days as they try to figure out who is spreading rumors. She says, "jonathan def told people. i heard something today and i know he told people."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Matthew refutes Jane's claim that Jonathan talked about it at a sorority gathering and tells her ... "I'll ask him - though it was definitely one of the upperclassmen in the room who told someone else and it spread."
      
    
            He asks, "Who told you this? If we can narrow down the girl we can narrow down suspects. I know it wasn't Jonathan. Trust me he would never."
      
    
            Jane says, "she wouldn't tell me who she heard it from cause it's one of her friends."
      
    
            Matthew tells her he's sorry and says, "these idiots will move on and it'll be done with."
      
    
            He talks to her about coming to the frat's upcoming Halloween party, but she later shoots back she "was uninvited" by the frat president ... and the tone of their conversation radically changes. She says "i knew this was going to happen. the woman will always get the short end of the stick. Yall aren't my friends. yall are covering your asses."
      
    
            On November 7, Mattew reaches out ... "My ex told me that I'm being labeled as an assaulter in the public eye, I was going to ask if you may have said something along those lines to someone but i know you wouldn't."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Jane denies saying anything and claims "people are changing the narrative because like in any sexual scenario w one woman and many men the woman was probably victim."
      
    
            She says ... "I know there are rumors I was gang banged."
      
    
            Jane says she mentioned Jonathan but never Matthew and he tells her, "Okay, I appreciate that a lot, thank you."
      
    
            He asks November 8th if they can talk, and she responds, "i think i'm done talking to you. i know you lied."
      
    
            Matthew replies, "What? Can you call?" She fires back, "no. never again."
      
    
            As we reported, on November 3rd, Jane texted Jonathan ... "let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn't know anyone in the room."

title: South Carolina Personal Trainer Elena Moore's Cause of Death Revealed, Watch Live
description:
South Carolina Personal Trainer
                          Elena Moore Cause of Death ...
body:
South Carolina Personal Trainer
                          Elena Moore Cause of Death ...
                          Authorities Announcing It Live
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 9, 2026
                            9:55 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 9, 2026
                                10:29 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Elena Katherine Moore's cause of death is about to be announced by local authorities in South Carolina ... and TMZ is streaming live.
      
    
            The Lexington County Coroner's office announced that officials will reveal the cause and manner of the personal trainer's death. You may remember, Elena was found dead in June about a week after she went missing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            A county spokesperson says Elena died from complications of cardiac dysrhythmia and premature ventricular contractions. It's considered to be natural causes. 
      

            Elena had a blood alcohol content of .089 during the autopsy -- though the spokesperson says it's unclear how body decomposition may have affected that number. She did not test positive for heart medication she was supposed to be using.
      
    
            Days before Elena went missing, the spokesperson says she was taken to a hospital where it was determined she was suffering a full mental health breakdown. She was put on an involuntary psychiatric hold.
      
    
            She's held in a medical facility until June 11 ... a total of 5 days. She's then released, and the spokesperson says Bannon Slice -- Elena's husband -- was contacted. Medical professionals put her in a cab, and she ended up stopping at a CVS where she procured 4 bottles of wine and a bottle of water.
      
    
            Worth noting ... Slice is not now and has never been considered a suspect in the case, the spokesperson also notes. In fact, the spokesperson is making a point to say her husband tried to help her navigate her physical and mental health challenges. 
      
    
            The spokesperson notes she had an irregular heartbeat and was also diagnosed with several mental health issues, including anxiety.
      
    
            Elena disappeared after leaving a Planet Fitness and heading toward a wooded area. Her husband reported her missing the following day.
      
    
            Days later, authorities found a body wearing clothes similar to Elena's ... and they later determined it was her. She was 39 years old.
      
    
            An autopsy was completed shortly after her death ... which investigators say revealed no bruising, cuts, gunshot wounds, stab wounds, blunt-force trauma, strangulation, or other external injuries.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We spoke to a friend of Elena's, who says she was acting paranoid in the weeks leading up to her death. She also shared a series of cryptic posts that seemed to indicate she was having issues with someone in her life.
      
    
            Another friend, Mendy Miller, told us she was well aware Elena had been on a fitness and health journey that included ridding herself of "toxic" people in her life, including friends.

schema.headline: South Carolina Personal Trainer Elena Moore's Cause of Death Revealed, Watch Live
